issues.legal_issue: A revisional court should not interfere at an interim stage with an appellate court’s order on additional evidence when the appellate court is acting within its jurisdiction and the appeal remains pending.
material_facts: During a first appeal from dismissal of a suit, the appellant asked to have a disputed will’s signature examined by a handwriting expert.
The first appellate court allowed the request for additional evidence.
While the appeal was still pending, the opposing party challenged that order in revision, and the High Court set it aside.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s revisional order was set aside, and the first appellate court was directed to decide the additional-evidence application afresh.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a revisional court should not interfere at an interim stage with an order made within the appellate court’s jurisdiction on an application under Order XLI Rule 27, particularly when the appeal remains pending and the challenged decision can be contested in accordance with law after the appellate decree. The Court relied on Mahavir Singh v. Naresh Chandra (2001) 1 SCC 309 and Gurdev Singh v. Mehnga Ram (1997) 6 SCC 507.

predicates.civil_appeal_pending: A civil appeal was pending before an appellate court.
predicates.appellate_court_ordered_additional_evide: The appellate court made an order on a party’s request to present additional evidence.
predicates.revision_challenged_interim_order: A party challenged that order in revision before the appeal had been finally decided.
predicates.revision_interference_set_aside_and_appl: The revisional interference is set aside and the appellate court is directed to reconsider the additional-evidence application.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal is pending and a party challenges an interim order on additional evidence in revision, the revisional interference is set aside and the application is remanded if the appellate court made an order on that evidence request.

issues.legal_issue: Additional evidence in an appeal may be admitted only on a prescribed ground, and the appellate court must assess whether it needs the evidence to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause rather than use it to fill a party’s evidentiary gaps.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought expert examination of the signature on a will during the first appeal, although no such application had been made at trial.
The plaintiff had not established that due diligence prevented him from seeking the examination before the trial court.
The first appellate court had allowed the application, but the Supreme Court did not decide whether the expert evidence should ultimately be admitted.
issues.conclusion: The application was remanded for the first appellate court to decide afresh under the applicable principles; the Supreme Court expressed no view on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: Section 107(1)(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Order XLI Rule 27, makes additional evidence exceptional: it may be allowed where evidence that ought to have been admitted was refused, where despite due diligence it was unavailable or could not be produced at trial, or where the appellate court requires it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. It cannot be used merely to patch weaknesses or fill gaps in a party’s case, and the court must record reasons for admitting it. The Court relied on K.R. Mohan Reddy v. Net Work Inc. (2007) 14 SCC 257, North Eastern Railway Admn. v. Bhagwan Das (2008) 8 SCC 511, N. Kamalam v. Ayyasamy (2001) 7 SCC 503, and Union of India v. Ibrahim Uddin (2012) 8 SCC 148.

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal was pending before an appellate court.
predicates.party_requests_additional_evidence: A party asked the appellate court to receive or obtain evidence not presented at trial.
predicates.appellate_court_must_reconsider_request_: The appellate court must decide the request by applying the exceptional grounds for additional evidence and whether the evidence is needed to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause.

issues.definition: When an appeal is pending and a party requests additional evidence, the appellate court must reconsider the request under the exceptional-evidence standard.
